screens.title: Securing Your Network: Security Groups and Network ACLs
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how two complementary AWS controls—Security Groups and Network ACLs—protect resources inside a VPC. Security Groups act as stateful, instance-level firewalls that only allow traffic you explicitly permit, while Network ACLs are stateless, subnet-level filters that can both allow and deny traffic and are evaluated in numeric order. Understanding their scopes and behaviors is essential for diagnosing connectivity problems and building layered defenses. We'll walk through a practical example: deploying a web server with a Security Group that permits SSH and HTTP, then creating a custom Network ACL for the public subnet that allows HTTP and the ephemeral ports needed for return traffic. You'll see how a missing ephemeral outbound rule in a stateless ACL can cause successful requests to time out. We'll also cover common mistakes to avoid, like using overly broad 0.0.0.0/0 rules for SSH, and the best practice of least privilege and role-specific Security Groups. By the end, you'll be able to design rulesets that minimize attack surface and troubleshoot access issues with confidence. Consider how you would block a single malicious IP for an entire subnet—this lesson shows the right tool and the correct configuration to do that.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Securing Your Network
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Security Groups & Network ACLs

Stateful instance-level controls meet stateless subnet filters. Learn when each is the right tool and how they work together to protect VPC resources.

In this lesson
Compare behaviors • Configure rules • Troubleshoot connectivity
Instance-level
Security Groups protect individual instances and resources.
Subnet-level
Network ACLs filter traffic in and out of subnets and support explicit denies.
Layered defence
Combine allow-only Security Groups with allow/deny NACLs for broad blocking rules.
Visual Overview
How they relate
Security Groups: stateful, instance. Network ACLs: stateless, subnet. Use both for defence in depth.
Explore Key Topics
Security Groups — instance rules, stateful responses, no explicit deny.
Network ACLs — subnet filters, stateless, explicit allow/deny, rule order matters.
Troubleshooting — ephemeral ports, rule order, and least privilege practice stop most issues.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to distinguish Security Groups from Network ACLs by scope, behavior, and evaluation order. You will design Security Group rules that follow the principle of least privilege and associate them correctly with EC2 instances to permit SSH, HTTP, or other protocols. You will configure Network ACLs for subnets, setting explicit allow and deny rules when required and accounting for their stateless behavior by adding matching return rules for ephemeral ports. You will also learn how to combine both controls so they work together: Security Groups as the primary instance firewall, and Network ACLs as a broad subnet filter for blocking malicious ranges or creating an additional enforcement boundary. Finally, you will be able to perform structured troubleshooting: verifying Security Group rules first, then examining Network ACL rules, rule numbers, and ephemeral port allowances to diagnose intermittent connectivity. These skills matter because misconfigured network controls are a common cause of incidents and outages; this chapter gives you the practical knowledge to prevent and resolve them.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice Tasks
screens.narratorSegment: These practice tasks map directly to the hands-on activity you'll perform. First, create a Security Group named WebTierSG that allows SSH from a specific admin IP and HTTP from the internet, launch an EC2 instance with that Security Group, and verify the web server responds. Second, build a custom Network ACL for the public subnet and add inbound and outbound rules for SSH, HTTP, and ephemeral ports so traffic can return to clients. Third, associate the custom Network ACL with the public subnet and observe how a denial rule immediately blocks traffic—then revert the rule to restore connectivity. Finally, complete a short troubleshooting checklist: confirm Security Group inbound rules, then confirm the Network ACL inbound and outbound rules and ensure ephemeral ports are allowed for return traffic. Successfully performing these tasks proves you can implement layered security without unintentionally disrupting service, and that you can identify whether instance-level or subnet-level controls are responsible for a connectivity problem.

Quick Checklist

  • 2. Network ACL inbound allows the same port for the subnet.
  • 3. Network ACL outbound allows ephemeral range for return traffic.
  • 4. Rule numbers evaluated low-to-high; first match applies.

screens.title: Security Groups: Instance-level, Stateful Firewalls
screens.narratorSegment: A Security Group is an instance-level virtual firewall that governs inbound and outbound traffic for EC2 instances and other ENI-associated resources. Its defining property is statefulness: when a connection is allowed in one direction, the return traffic for that connection is permitted automatically, even if there is no explicit rule for the return path. Practically, this means if you allow inbound HTTP to port 80, responses to clients are permitted without a separate outbound rule. Security Group rules are permit-only; you cannot write explicit deny rules. If traffic isn't explicitly allowed, it is implicitly denied. You can associate multiple Security Groups with a single instance and the combined set of allowed rules across groups determines permitted traffic. A common, practical pattern is to create role-specific groups like WebServerSG and DatabaseSG and restrict sources to only what they need — for example, allow MySQL from the DatabaseSG rather than opening a CIDR block. A common misconception is thinking Security Groups can block traffic; they only allow. Another pitfall is using overly broad sources such as 0.0.0.0/0 for SSH, which increases risk. Key takeaway: use narrow sources, group-by-role, and rely on the stateful nature to keep rules simple while minimizing the attack surface.

keyIdea.title: Security Group insight
keyIdea.text: Security Groups are stateful, instance-focused, allow-only firewalls—design them by role, and avoid wide open sources for critical ports.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Security Groups
Definition

What a Security Group does

Security Groups control inbound and outbound traffic for instances. They are stateful and permit return traffic automatically.

Stateful behavior
No separate rule needed for responses; connection tracking handles it.
Allow-only rules
If a port isn't allowed, traffic is implicitly denied.
Combined group rules example
If WebSG allows HTTP and AdminSG allows SSH, attaching both groups to the same instance permits both services without merging rules manually.
Example scenario
You open port 80 inbound for a web server. Clients connect and the server's replies flow automatically because the Security Group is stateful. You do not need a matching outbound rule for the client's ephemeral port.
Common mistakes
  • Opening SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 instead of limiting to admin IPs.
  • Expecting Security Groups to block traffic; they only allow.
  • Forgetting to attach any Security Group to a new instance.
Key Takeaway

Use Security Groups as your instance firewall, keep rules narrow, and create role-based groups for clarity.

Check your understanding
If inbound HTTP is allowed but clients can't see the page, first verify the Security Group allows port 80 from the client's source IP before digging into NACLs.

screens.title: Network ACLs: Subnet-level, Stateless Filters
screens.narratorSegment: A Network Access Control List operates at the subnet boundary and offers an optional, coarse-grained layer of security for VPC traffic. Unlike Security Groups, Network ACLs are stateless: when you allow inbound traffic, you must explicitly permit the corresponding outbound return traffic with a separate rule. This requirement is crucial when you expose services to the internet because clients use ephemeral source ports for their side of the connection. If the NACL lacks the outbound ephemeral-range allowance, the server can receive requests but will fail to send responses, causing timeouts. Network ACLs support both allow and deny rules and evaluate entries by ascending rule number; the first matching rule is applied and no further rules are checked for that packet. New custom Network ACLs default to deny-all until you add rules, while the VPC default NACL initially allows all. Use NACLs when you need to block or explicitly deny traffic across an entire subnet, for example to refuse a known malicious CIDR across many instances. Be mindful: because they are stateless and ordered, NACLs are powerful but also error-prone if you forget return rules or mis-order your rule numbers.

keyIdea.title: NACL insight
keyIdea.text: Network ACLs are stateless, ordered, and can explicitly deny traffic—use them for subnet-wide filters and explicit blocks, remembering to allow return ephemeral ports.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Network ACLs
Definition & Behavior

Stateless subnet filter

Network ACLs require explicit rules for both directions. Rule order is critical and denies can be added to block ranges at subnet scale.

Allow and Deny
NACLs can explicitly deny traffic, making them useful for blocking known bad IPs.
Rule ordering
Rules are evaluated from the lowest number upward; the first match is applied.
Example: ephemeral ports
If inbound port 80 is allowed, you must also add outbound allow for ephemeral 1024-65535 so the server can send responses to clients' ephemeral ports.
Configuration tips
  • Start with explicit allow rules and keep a final deny-all rule.
  • Use low-numbered rules for broad denies you want to match first.
  • Remember to add matching outbound rules for return traffic in stateless systems.
Pitfall

Failing to allow ephemeral ranges outbound will cause successful incoming connections to hang because responses are blocked at the subnet boundary.

Key Takeaway

Use NACLs for explicit subnet-wide denies and broad filtering, and always account for stateless return rules.

screens.title: Stateful vs Stateless: Why Return Traffic Is Different
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding stateful versus stateless behavior is central to avoiding connectivity surprises. Stateful systems, such as Security Groups, automatically track connections and permit return traffic. Stateless systems, like Network ACLs, do not maintain connection state; each packet is evaluated independently against rules. Consider a simple web server: when a client sends an HTTP request from a random ephemeral source port, the server responds to that ephemeral port. With a Security Group that allows inbound port 80, the return is automatically allowed. With a Network ACL, you must add an outbound rule that allows traffic to ephemeral ports so the response can leave the subnet. A common real-world symptom is intermittent access: packets arrive, the server processes them, but responses cannot leave because ephemeral ports are blocked in the NACL outbound rules, producing timeouts. Another contrast is scope: Security Groups attach to instances and combine permissive rules, while NACLs attach to subnets and are ordered. Misconception to avoid: stateful does not mean permissive by default—Security Groups still require explicit allow rules. Key takeaway: always account for ephemeral return traffic when you use stateless filters.

keyIdea.text: Stateful Security Groups simplify two-way flows; stateless NACLs require explicit rules in both directions, especially for ephemeral port ranges.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Stateful vs Stateless
Stateful (Security Groups)
Automatically allow return traffic for established connections. Attach to instances. Rules are allow-only.
  • Example: Inbound HTTP allowed → response flows without outbound rule.
  • Best practice: narrow source CIDRs and use group references for internal traffic.
Stateless (Network ACLs)
Evaluate each packet independently. Provide matching rules for inbound and outbound, including ephemeral ranges.
  • Example: Allow inbound HTTP but forget outbound ephemeral → requests time out.
  • Rule order matters: first matching rule applies; default deny at the end blocks non-matching traffic.
Analogy
Think of Security Groups as a door guard who remembers guests; Network ACLs are a checkpoint that inspects each plate independently.
Misconception check
Stateful does not remove the need for good rules. You must still explicitly allow required ports on Security Groups.

screens.title: Designing Security Group Rules — A Practical Process
screens.narratorSegment: Designing Security Group rules is best done with a stepwise approach to minimize risk. Start by defining the role of the instances: web server, application server, or database. For each role, list required ports and trusted sources. For example, a web server needs TCP port 80 open from 0.0.0.0/0 for general access, but SSH should be limited to your admin IP or a bastion host. Next, create one Security Group per role rather than opening multiple services in a single group. This makes intent clear and simplifies auditing. Where possible, use Security Group references instead of CIDR blocks for internal traffic—allow the DatabaseSG to accept MySQL only from WebSG. After creating rules, attach the Security Group to instances and verify connectivity from expected source addresses only. Finally, review outbound rules and narrow them where practical; though Security Groups are stateful, restricting outbound traffic reduces exfiltration risks. A common mistake is attaching overly permissive groups to instances or forgetting to remove default groups with broad allowances. Key takeaway: adopt a minimal role-based pattern, test with least privilege, and iterate by adding only what proves necessary.

keyIdea.text: Create role-specific Security Groups, prefer group references for internal traffic, restrict admin access to known IPs, and test least privilege.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Design Security Group Rules
Step-by-step
  1. 1. Identify role and required ports (e.g., web: 80, ssh: 22).
  2. 2. Limit sources: use specific admin IPs or internal group references.
  3. 3. Create one SG per role and attach to instances.
  4. 4. Verify connectivity from trusted sources and adjust minimally.
  5. 5. Harden outbound rules where appropriate to prevent exfiltration.
Concrete example
WebTierSG: inbound TCP 80 from 0.0.0.0/0, inbound TCP 22 from admin CIDR only. DatabaseSG: inbound MySQL from WebTierSG only.
Analyst tip
Name and tag Security Groups to indicate intent; this speeds debugging when incidents happen.
Key Takeaway
Design for least privilege, test from the expected source, and use group references for secure internal communication.

screens.title: Configuring a Network ACL for a Public Subnet
screens.narratorSegment: When configuring a Network ACL for a public web subnet, follow an ordered rule plan. Create the custom NACL and then add inbound rules: allow SSH from your admin IP at a low number, allow HTTP from the internet, and allow the ephemeral port range so responses can reach client ephemeral ports. Use rule numbers to ensure broad denies or blocks are evaluated first when needed. For outbound rules, add matching entries: allow HTTP and HTTPS as needed and allow ephemeral ports outbound to let server responses traverse to clients' ephemeral ports. Keep the default deny rule at the end to catch anything not matched. A practical example from the chapter: inbound rule 100 open SSH from a specific CIDR, rule 110 allow HTTP 80 from 0.0.0.0/0, and rule 120 allow custom TCP 1024-65535 from 0.0.0.0/0 for return traffic. For outbound add rules that allow ephemeral ports and any specific protocol your instance initiates. When you deny or remove the HTTP allow, traffic is immediately blocked even if the Security Group allows it. This demonstrates the power of subnet-level filtering and the importance of correct ordering and return rules.

keyIdea.title: NACL configuration
keyIdea.text: Add ordered inbound and outbound allow rules for service ports and ephemeral ranges; place a deny-all at the end to limit unexpected traffic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Configuring NACL
Recommended rule sequence
Inbound rules (example)
  • Rule 100: Allow TCP 22 from Admin CIDR
  • Rule 110: Allow TCP 80 from 0.0.0.0/0
  • Rule 120: Allow TCP 1024-65535 from 0.0.0.0/0 (for return traffic)
  • Rule *: Deny all remaining traffic
Outbound rules (example)
  • Rule 100: Allow TCP 80 to 0.0.0.0/0 (if instance initiates)
  • Rule 110: Allow TCP 443 to 0.0.0.0/0
  • Rule 120: Allow TCP 1024-65535 to 0.0.0.0/0 (responses to clients)
  • Rule *: Deny all remaining traffic
Why rule order matters
First match wins. Place intentional denies or specific blocks at lower numbers to ensure they are applied before general allows.
Common pitfall
Forgetting to allow ephemeral ports in the outbound rules causes the web server to accept requests but not send responses.
Key Takeaway
Treat NACLs as ordered filters and always add matching return rules when you allow inbound connections.

screens.title: Hands-on Walkthrough: Launching a Web Server with User Data
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough demonstrates the practical commands and the user data script used to install a web server on launch. User data script (bash)
#!/bin/bash
yum update -y
yum install -y nginx
systemctl start nginx
systemctl enable nginx
echo "<h1>Hello from WebInstanceWithSG!</h1>" > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
Verification commands (SSH)
# Check nginx status
sudo systemctl status nginx

# Confirm port listening
sudo ss -tuln | grep :80
Troubleshooting hints
  • Confirm Security Group inbound allows port 80 from the client source.
  • Check NACL inbound for port 80 and NACL outbound for ephemeral 1024-65535.
  • Verify instance has a public IP and auto-assign is enabled on the subnet.
Key Takeaway
Bootstrapping with user data speeds validation, but always verify both SG and NACL rules when connectivity fails.

screens.title: Diagnosing Connectivity: A Step-by-step Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: When connectivity fails, use a consistent checklist to find the culprit quickly. Step one: confirm the instance has a healthy OS and your service is running—use systemctl or process checks. Step two: verify the Security Group inbound rule allows the expected port from the expected source; check for multiple attached groups that may open or restrict ports. Step three: if Security Groups look correct, inspect the Network ACL associated with the subnet. Because NACLs are stateless, check both inbound and outbound rules—make sure ephemeral ports (typically 1024–65535) are allowed in the outbound direction when clients initiate connections. Step four: review rule ordering and explicit deny entries in the NACL; a low-numbered deny will block traffic even if later rules allow it. Step five: confirm route tables and internet gateway attachments for public subnets and that the instance has a public IP if required. Common pitfalls include forgetting ephemeral outbound NACL rules and using broad 0.0.0.0/0 allowances during troubleshooting in production. Finally, after fixing the rule, test end-to-end and then harden rules back to least privilege. Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Diagnosing Connectivity
Step-by-step diagnosis
1. Service health

Confirm the process is running and listening on the expected port.

2. Security Group rules

Verify inbound rules allow the port and correct CIDR. Check all attached SGs and combined effects.

3. Network ACL rules

Inspect inbound and outbound rules, ephemeral ranges, and rule order for explicit denies.

4. Routing & IP

Ensure route tables and internet gateway exist and the instance has a public IP if needed.

5. Test and revert

Make minimal rule changes to test, then harden rules back to least privilege once validated.

Scenario
If SSH works but HTTP times out, check Security Group for port 80, then the NACL inbound for port 80 and outbound for ephemeral ports. Often ephemeral outbound is missing.

screens.title: Layered Security: Combining Security Groups and NACLs
screens.narratorSegment: A layered approach reduces risk by applying controls at multiple levels. Use Security Groups as your primary defensive layer: they are easy to manage, stateful, and ideal for role-specific policies. Add Network ACLs where you need broad, subnet-wide rules—useful to block known malicious IP ranges or to implement an extra deny for an entire subnet. For example, keep WebTierSG on web instances to permit HTTP only and DatabaseSG for database instances to allow MySQL only from the web group. Then, apply a custom NACL to the public subnet that denies a blacklisted CIDR at a low rule number while allowing the service ports and ephemeral return ports. This way, even if a Security Group is misconfigured, the NACL can block traffic at the subnet edge. But be cautious: NACLs are stateless and ordered, so they add complexity and potential for errors. Use NACLs sparingly for broad rules and rely on Security Groups for day-to-day instance protections. Key takeaway: defense in depth is effective when each layer has clear intent and minimal overlap that could create management confusion. Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Layered Security
Pattern: Roles + Subnet Filter
  • Assign WebTierSG to web instances allowing HTTP and limited SSH.
  • Assign DatabaseSG to database instances allowing DB ports only from WebTierSG.
  • Attach a NACL to the public subnet to deny known malicious CIDRs and allow required service and ephemeral ranges.
Practical example
If an attacker IP is discovered, add a deny rule in the NACL to block that CIDR for the whole subnet. Security Groups still manage legitimate instance-level access.
Benefit
Defense in depth: even if an SG is mis-applied, the NACL can stop broad threats.
Caution
Avoid duplicative complex rules across layers; document intent to prevent operational errors.
Key Takeaway
Layered controls work best when each layer has a single clear purpose: instance allow vs subnet block.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Several repeated mistakes lead to avoidable outages and security gaps. First, opening SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 is too permissive; prefer admin IPs or a bastion host. Second, neglecting ephemeral return rules in Network ACLs produces intermittent connectivity where requests succeed but responses are blocked. Third, mis-ordered NACL rules or an unintended low-numbered deny can silently block traffic even when Security Groups allow it. Fourth, relying on temporary broad-open rules for troubleshooting in production can create windows of exposure—test with specific rules and revert promptly. Best practices include: follow the principle of least privilege, use role-specific Security Groups, reference Security Groups for internal traffic, limit NACL usage to explicit blocking scenarios, and document changes to both SGs and NACLs with reason and rollback steps. Regularly audit rule sets to remove unused or stale entries. Finally, when you troubleshoot, follow a reproducible checklist so you change only what's needed and can revert. These habits prevent many common incidents and keep the VPC secure while maintaining availability. Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Common Mistakes & Best Practices
Mistake: Broad SSH access
Opening SSH to the world creates unnecessary attack surface.
Mistake: Forgetting ephemeral rules
Stateless NACLs require both inbound and outbound rules for successful two-way connections.
Practice: Least privilege
Grant only necessary ports and sources, and use security group references for internal services.
Operational guidance
  • Document rule changes and include rollback steps.
  • Audit rules regularly and remove stale entries.
  • During troubleshooting, make minimal and reversible changes.
Key Takeaway
Well-documented, minimal rules across Security Groups and NACLs keep systems secure and reliable.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the core ideas you should remember. First, a Security Group is a stateful, instance-level virtual firewall that permits traffic you explicitly allow; it does not support explicit denies. Second, a Network ACL is a stateless, subnet-level filter that evaluates rules in ascending numeric order and supports both allow and deny actions. Third, ephemeral ports—typically 1024 to 65535—are used by client endpoints and must be allowed in NACL outbound rules to enable return traffic when NACLs are used. These three concepts—scope, statefulness, and return-port behavior—explain most real-world connectivity puzzles when you work with VPC networking. Keep these definitions handy when designing or debugging rules so you can quickly identify whether instance-level or subnet-level controls are the right place to make a change. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how two complementary AWS controls—Security Groups and Network ACLs—protect resources inside a VPC. Security Groups act as stateful, instance-level firewalls that only allow traffic you explicitly permit, while Network ACLs are stateless, subnet-level filters that can both allow and deny traffic and are evaluated in numeric order. Understanding their scopes and behaviors is essential for diagnosing connectivity problems and building layered defenses. We'll walk through a practical example: deploying a web server with a Security Group that permits SSH and HTTP, then creating a custom Network ACL for the public subnet that allows HTTP and the ephemeral ports needed for return traffic. You'll see how a missing ephemeral outbound rule in a stateless ACL can cause successful requests to time out. We'll also cover common mistakes to avoid, like using overly broad 0.0.0.0/0 rules for SSH, and the best practice of least privilege and role-specific Security Groups. By the end, you'll be able to design rulesets that minimize attack surface and troubleshoot access issues with confidence. Consider how you would block a single malicious IP for an entire subnet—this lesson shows the right tool and the correct configuration to do that.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to distinguish Security Groups from Network ACLs by scope, behavior, and evaluation order. You will design Security Group rules that follow the principle of least privilege and associate them correctly with EC2 instances to permit SSH, HTTP, or other protocols. You will configure Network ACLs for subnets, setting explicit allow and deny rules when required and accounting for their stateless behavior by adding matching return rules for ephemeral ports. You will also learn how to combine both controls so they work together: Security Groups as the primary instance firewall, and Network ACLs as a broad subnet filter for blocking malicious ranges or creating an additional enforcement boundary. Finally, you will be able to perform structured troubleshooting: verifying Security Group rules first, then examining Network ACL rules, rule numbers, and ephemeral port allowances to diagnose intermittent connectivity. These skills matter because misconfigured network controls are a common cause of incidents and outages; this chapter gives you the practical knowledge to prevent and resolve them.

These practice tasks map directly to the hands-on activity you'll perform. First, create a Security Group named WebTierSG that allows SSH from a specific admin IP and HTTP from the internet, launch an EC2 instance with that Security Group, and verify the web server responds. Second, build a custom Network ACL for the public subnet and add inbound and outbound rules for SSH, HTTP, and ephemeral ports so traffic can return to clients. Third, associate the custom Network ACL with the public subnet and observe how a denial rule immediately blocks traffic—then revert the rule to restore connectivity. Finally, complete a short troubleshooting checklist: confirm Security Group inbound rules, then confirm the Network ACL inbound and outbound rules and ensure ephemeral ports are allowed for return traffic. Successfully performing these tasks proves you can implement layered security without unintentionally disrupting service, and that you can identify whether instance-level or subnet-level controls are responsible for a connectivity problem.

A Security Group is an instance-level virtual firewall that governs inbound and outbound traffic for EC2 instances and other ENI-associated resources. Its defining property is statefulness: when a connection is allowed in one direction, the return traffic for that connection is permitted automatically, even if there is no explicit rule for the return path. Practically, this means if you allow inbound HTTP to port 80, responses to clients are permitted without a separate outbound rule. Security Group rules are permit-only; you cannot write explicit deny rules. If traffic isn't explicitly allowed, it is implicitly denied. You can associate multiple Security Groups with a single instance and the combined set of allowed rules across groups determines permitted traffic. A common, practical pattern is to create role-specific groups like WebServerSG and DatabaseSG and restrict sources to only what they need — for example, allow MySQL from the DatabaseSG rather than opening a CIDR block. A common misconception is thinking Security Groups can block traffic; they only allow. Another pitfall is using overly broad sources such as 0.0.0.0/0 for SSH, which increases risk. Key takeaway: use narrow sources, group-by-role, and rely on the stateful nature to keep rules simple while minimizing the attack surface.

A Network Access Control List operates at the subnet boundary and offers an optional, coarse-grained layer of security for VPC traffic. Unlike Security Groups, Network ACLs are stateless: when you allow inbound traffic, you must explicitly permit the corresponding outbound return traffic with a separate rule. This requirement is crucial when you expose services to the internet because clients use ephemeral source ports for their side of the connection. If the NACL lacks the outbound ephemeral-range allowance, the server can receive requests but will fail to send responses, causing timeouts. Network ACLs support both allow and deny rules and evaluate entries by ascending rule number; the first matching rule is applied and no further rules are checked for that packet. New custom Network ACLs default to deny-all until you add rules, while the VPC default NACL initially allows all. Use NACLs when you need to block or explicitly deny traffic across an entire subnet, for example to refuse a known malicious CIDR across many instances. Be mindful: because they are stateless and ordered, NACLs are powerful but also error-prone if you forget return rules or mis-order your rule numbers.

Understanding stateful versus stateless behavior is central to avoiding connectivity surprises. Stateful systems, such as Security Groups, automatically track connections and permit return traffic. Stateless systems, like Network ACLs, do not maintain connection state; each packet is evaluated independently against rules. Consider a simple web server: when a client sends an HTTP request from a random ephemeral source port, the server responds to that ephemeral port. With a Security Group that allows inbound port 80, the return is automatically allowed. With a Network ACL, you must add an outbound rule that allows traffic to ephemeral ports so the response can leave the subnet. A common real-world symptom is intermittent access: packets arrive, the server processes them, but responses cannot leave because ephemeral ports are blocked in the NACL outbound rules, producing timeouts. Another contrast is scope: Security Groups attach to instances and combine permissive rules, while NACLs attach to subnets and are ordered. Misconception to avoid: stateful does not mean permissive by default—Security Groups still require explicit allow rules. Key takeaway: always account for ephemeral return traffic when you use stateless filters.

Designing Security Group rules is best done with a stepwise approach to minimize risk. Start by defining the role of the instances: web server, application server, or database. For each role, list required ports and trusted sources. For example, a web server needs TCP port 80 open from 0.0.0.0/0 for general access, but SSH should be limited to your admin IP or a bastion host. Next, create one Security Group per role rather than opening multiple services in a single group. This makes intent clear and simplifies auditing. Where possible, use Security Group references instead of CIDR blocks for internal traffic—allow the DatabaseSG to accept MySQL only from WebSG. After creating rules, attach the Security Group to instances and verify connectivity from expected source addresses only. Finally, review outbound rules and narrow them where practical; though Security Groups are stateful, restricting outbound traffic reduces exfiltration risks. A common mistake is attaching overly permissive groups to instances or forgetting to remove default groups with broad allowances. Key takeaway: adopt a minimal role-based pattern, test with least privilege, and iterate by adding only what proves necessary.

When configuring a Network ACL for a public web subnet, follow an ordered rule plan. Create the custom NACL and then add inbound rules: allow SSH from your admin IP at a low number, allow HTTP from the internet, and allow the ephemeral port range so responses can reach client ephemeral ports. Use rule numbers to ensure broad denies or blocks are evaluated first when needed. For outbound rules, add matching entries: allow HTTP and HTTPS as needed and allow ephemeral ports outbound to let server responses traverse to clients' ephemeral ports. Keep the default deny rule at the end to catch anything not matched. A practical example from the chapter: inbound rule 100 open SSH from a specific CIDR, rule 110 allow HTTP 80 from 0.0.0.0/0, and rule 120 allow custom TCP 1024-65535 from 0.0.0.0/0 for return traffic. For outbound add rules that allow ephemeral ports and any specific protocol your instance initiates. When you deny or remove the HTTP allow, traffic is immediately blocked even if the Security Group allows it. This demonstrates the power of subnet-level filtering and the importance of correct ordering and return rules.

The provided script updates the instance, installs Nginx, starts it, and writes a simple index page. In the console you create WebTierSG with inbound SSH limited to your IP and inbound HTTP open to the internet, then launch an instance using that Security Group and include this script as user data.
